questions.stem: A model $\hat y = wx$ with **no intercept** is fitted by least squares to the three points $(1, 3)$, $(2, 5)$ and $(3, 8)$. The value of $w$ is ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: Used $\sum y/\sum x = 16/6$, a ratio of totals, instead of $\sum xy/\sum x^2$.
Computed the slope $S_{xy}/S_{xx}$ of the line with intercept; this model has no intercept.
Inverted the formula: $\sum x^2/\sum xy = 14/37$.

questions.solution:
1. Setting $\frac{d}{dw}\sum (y - wx)^2 = 0$ gives $w = \sum xy/\sum x^2$.
2. $\sum xy = 3 + 10 + 24 = 37$, $\sum x^2 = 1 + 4 + 9 = 14$.
3. $w = 37/14 \approx 2.64$.

questions.stem: For $n = 4$ points the sums are $\sum x = 8$, $\sum y = 22$, $\sum x^2 = 20$, $\sum xy = 50$. A least squares line **through the origin**, $\hat y = wx$, is fitted. Its prediction at $x = 3$ is

options.why: Took $w = \sum y/\sum x = 2.75$; the least squares slope weights each point by its $x$.
Inverted the ratio: $w = 20/50 = 0.4$.
Fitted the line with intercept ($b = 1.5$, $a = 2.5$); the model here is forced through the origin.

questions.solution:
1. Only $\sum xy$ and $\sum x^2$ matter for a no-intercept fit: $w = 50/20 = 2.5$.
2. $\hat y(3) = 2.5 \times 3 = 7.5$. ($\sum x$ and $\sum y$ would be needed only with an intercept.)

questions.stem:
The model $\hat y = w/x$ (one parameter $w$, no intercept) is fitted by least squares to

| $x$ | 1 | 2 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ | 4 | 2.5 | 1 |

The value of $w$ is ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: Fitted $\hat y = wx$ instead ($13/21$); the feature here is $\phi(x) = 1/x$.
Used $\sum\phi y/\sum\phi = 5.5/1.75$; the denominator must be $\sum\phi^2$.
Used $\sum y/\sum\phi = 7.5/1.75$, a ratio of totals.

questions.stem: The model $\hat y = wx$ (no intercept) is fitted by least squares to the points $(1, 2)$, $(2, 2)$, $(3, 6)$. Let $e_i = y_i - wx_i$. Which statements are true?

options.why: Without an intercept only $\sum x_ie_i = 0$ is guaranteed; here $\sum e_i = 10 - 6w = -2/7$.

options.text: Adding a fourth point $(0, 5)$ leaves $w$ unchanged
options.why: A point with $x = 0$ adds $0$ to both $\sum xy$ and $\sum x^2$, so the line through the origin cannot react to it.
$\hat y(2) = 24/7 \approx 3.43 > 2$, so $e = -10/7$; a positive value comes from computing $\hat y - y$.

questions.solution:
1. $w = \sum xy/\sum x^2 = 24/14 = 12/7 \approx 1.714$.
2. Residuals: $2/7$, $-10/7$, $6/7$. Their sum is $-2/7 \ne 0$, but $\sum xe = 2/7 - 20/7 + 18/7 = 0$.
3. A point $(0, y)$ adds nothing to $\sum xy$ or $\sum x^2$, so $w$ stays $12/7$.

questions.stem: The model $\hat y = wx$ (no intercept) is fitted by least squares to the points $(1, 1)$, $(2, 4)$ and $(3, k)$. The fitted slope turns out to be exactly $w = 2$. The value of $k$ is ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: Used $w = \sum y/\sum x$: $(5 + k)/6 = 2$.
Assumed the third point lies on the line $y = 2x$; least squares does not force any point onto the line.
Used $\sum x = 6$ in the denominator instead of $\sum x^2 = 14$.

questions.stem: For the no-intercept loss $L(w) = \sum_i (y_i - wx_i)^2$, the derivative $\dfrac{dL}{dw}$ is

options.why: Dropped the inner factor $x_i$; this is the derivative with respect to an intercept, not the slope.
Lost the minus sign of the inner derivative $-x_i$.
Chain rule: the derivative of $y_i - wx_i$ with respect to $w$ is $-x_i$.
Multiplied by $x_i$ twice; the chain rule contributes one factor $x_i$.

questions.solution:
1. $\frac{d}{dw}(y_i - wx_i)^2 = 2(y_i - wx_i)(-x_i)$.
2. Sum: $dL/dw = -2\sum x_i(y_i - wx_i)$. Setting it to 0 gives $\sum x_iy_i = w\sum x_i^2$.

questions.stem: On the same data, a line through the origin $\hat y = wx$ and a line with intercept $\hat y = a + bx$ are both fitted by least squares. Let $\text{SSE}_0$ and $\text{SSE}_1$ be their minimum sums of squared residuals. Which statement is **always** true?

options.why: Direction reversed: a fit with fewer free parameters cannot beat the minimum over a larger set.
Equality holds only when the best intercept happens to be 0; not always.

options.text: Either one can be smaller, depending on the data
options.why: Minimising over all $(a, b)$ includes $(0, w)$, so $\text{SSE}_1$ can never exceed $\text{SSE}_0$.
The origin model is the special case $a = 0$ of the intercept model, so the larger model does at least as well.

questions.solution:
1. Every origin line $y = wx$ is also a line $a + bx$ with $a = 0$.
2. $\text{SSE}_1$ is a minimum over a set that contains all origin lines, so $\text{SSE}_1 \le \text{SSE}_0$, with equality only when the best intercept is 0.

questions.stem:
A line $\hat y = a + bx$ is fitted by ordinary least squares to

| $x$ | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ | 3 | 7 | 8 | 12 |

The slope $b$ is ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: Used the no-intercept formula $\sum xy/\sum x^2 = 178/120$; with an intercept the sums must be centred.
Inverted the ratio: $S_{xx}/S_{xy} = 20/28$.
Divided by $S_{yy} = 41$ instead of $S_{xx} = 20$ (that is the slope of $x$ on $y$).

questions.stem: For a simple linear regression $\hat y = a + bx$ fitted by least squares, the sample means are $\bar x = 10$, $\bar y = 50$ and the fitted slope is $b = 3$. The prediction at $x = 12$ is

options.why: Used $\hat y = bx$ and forgot the intercept $a = \bar y - b\bar x = 20$.
Used $\bar y + bx$ instead of $\bar y + b(x - \bar x)$; $x$ must be measured from $\bar x$.
The line passes through $(\bar x, \bar y)$: $\hat y = 50 + 3(12 - 10) = 56$.
Took $a = \bar y + b\bar x = 80$; the sign in $a = \bar y - b\bar x$ was flipped.

questions.solution:
1. With an intercept the line passes through $(\bar x, \bar y)$, so $a = \bar y - b\bar x = 50 - 30 = 20$.
2. $\hat y(12) = 20 + 3 \times 12 = 56$, the same as $50 + 3(12 - 10)$.

questions.stem: A least squares line $\hat y = a + bx$ is fitted to $n = 5$ points with centred sums $S_{xx} = \sum(x - \bar x)^2 = 10$, $S_{yy} = \sum(y - \bar y)^2 = 50$ and $S_{xy} = \sum(x - \bar x)(y - \bar y) = 20$. The residual sum of squares $\text{SSE} = \sum (y_i - \hat y_i)^2$ is ______.

traps.why: Gave the explained sum of squares $S_{xy}^2/S_{xx}$, not what is left over.
Subtracted $S_{xy}$ itself ($50 - 20$); the explained part is $b\,S_{xy} = S_{xy}^2/S_{xx}$.
Computed $1 - R^2$, the unexplained fraction, not the sum of squares.

questions.stem: An OLS line $\hat y = a + bx$ with $b \ne 0$ is fitted to some data. Every target is then transformed to $y' = 2y + 3$ (the $x_i$ unchanged) and the line is refitted as $\hat y' = a' + b'x$. Which statements are true?

options.why: $S_{xy}$ doubles (the $+3$ cancels when centring) while $S_{xx}$ is unchanged.
$R^2 = S_{xy}^2/(S_{xx}S_{yy})$: both $S_{xy}^2$ and $S_{yy}$ scale by 4, so $R^2$ is unchanged.
$a' = \bar y' - b'\bar x = 2\bar y + 3 - 2b\bar x = 2a + 3$.

options.text: The residual sum of squares doubles
options.why: Each residual doubles, so each squared residual is multiplied by 4; SSE becomes $4\,\text{SSE}$.

questions.solution:
1. Fitted values transform the same way: $\hat y' = 2\hat y + 3$, so $b' = 2b$ and $a' = 2a + 3$.
2. Residuals $e' = y' - \hat y' = 2e$, so SSE is multiplied by 4, and so is $S_{yy}$.
3. $R^2 = 1 - \text{SSE}/S_{yy}$ is unchanged.

questions.stem: On the same data, regressing $y$ on $x$ by least squares gives slope $b_{y|x} = 0.8$, and regressing $x$ on $y$ gives slope $b_{x|y} = 0.45$. The coefficient of determination $R^2$ (the same for both fits) is

options.why: Gave the correlation $r = \sqrt{0.36}$; $R^2$ is the product of the slopes itself.
Divided the slopes ($0.8/0.45$); that ratio is $S_{yy}/S_{xx}$, not $R^2$.
Squared only $b_{y|x}$; $b^2$ equals $R^2$ only when $S_{xx} = S_{yy}$.
$b_{y|x}\,b_{x|y} = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}\cdot\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{yy}} = r^2 = 0.8 \times 0.45$.

questions.stem:
An OLS line $\hat y = a + bx$ is fitted to

| $x$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ | 2 | 4 | 5 | 4 | 5 |

The predicted value at $x = 6$ is ______ (round to one decimal).

traps.why: Fitted through the origin ($w = 66/55 = 1.2$); this model has an intercept.
Inverted the slope ($S_{xx}/S_{xy} = 10/6$), which gives $a = -1$.
Used $a = \bar y + b\bar x$ (sign slip) and then added $6b$.
Reported the intercept $a$, not the prediction at $x = 6$.

questions.stem: No-intercept ridge regression minimises $\sum_i (y_i - wx_i)^2 + \lambda w^2$ with $\lambda = 6$ on the data $(1, 1)$, $(2, 3)$, $(3, 4)$. Using the fitted $w$, the prediction at $x = 4$ is ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: Ignored the penalty: the OLS weight $19/14$ gives $5.43$.
Used $\sum x^2 + 2\lambda$ in the denominator; the factor 2 appears in both derivative terms and cancels.
Added $\lambda^2 = 36$ instead of $\lambda$ to the denominator.
Reported $w$ instead of the prediction $4w$.

questions.stem: A ridge model $\hat y = b + wx$ is fitted with the usual convention: the intercept $b$ is **not** penalised, only $\lambda w^2$ is. As $\lambda \to \infty$, the prediction $\hat y$ for every $x$ tends to

options.why: That happens only if the intercept is also penalised (or absent); here $b$ is free.

options.text: $\bar y$, the mean of the training targets
options.why: $w \to 0$, and the free intercept then minimises $\sum (y_i - b)^2$, giving $b = \bar y$.
Direction reversed: OLS is the limit $\lambda \to 0$, not $\lambda \to \infty$.

options.text: The median of the training targets
options.why: Squared loss is minimised by the mean; the median minimises absolute loss.

questions.solution:
1. A huge $\lambda$ forces $w \to 0$ (never exactly 0 for finite $\lambda$).
2. With $w = 0$ the loss is $\sum (y_i - b)^2$, minimised at $b = \bar y$.
3. So every prediction tends to $\bar y$: a flat line.

questions.stem:
A ridge fit with two standardised features and no intercept has
$$X^\top X = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \quad X^\top y = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \lambda = 1.$$
The first weight $w_1$ of $w = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y$ is ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: Ignored $\lambda$: the OLS solution is $(2, 0)$.
Added $\lambda$ to every entry of $X^\top X$ instead of only the diagonal ($\lambda I$).
Ignored the off-diagonal 1 and divided $4/(2 + 1)$ as if $X^\top X$ were diagonal.
Added $2\lambda$ to the diagonal.

questions.solution:
1. $X^\top X + I = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$, determinant $9 - 1 = 8$.
2. Inverse $= \frac{1}{8}\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$.
3. $w = \frac{1}{8}(12 - 2,\ -4 + 6) = (1.25,\ 0.25)$, so $w_1 = 1.25$.

questions.stem: One feature, no intercept, data with $\sum x_iy_i > 0$. Let $w_0$ be the OLS weight and $w_\lambda = \arg\min_w \sum (y_i - wx_i)^2 + \lambda w^2$ for some $\lambda > 0$. Which statements are true?

options.why: $w_\lambda = \sum xy/(\sum x^2 + \lambda)$ has the same positive numerator as $w_0$ and a larger denominator.

options.text: The training SSE $\sum (y_i - w_\lambda x_i)^2$ is at least the training SSE of $w_0$
options.why: $w_0$ minimises the SSE, so any other weight, including $w_\lambda$, gives an SSE at least as large.

options.text: For a large enough $\lambda$, $w_\lambda$ becomes negative
options.why: Numerator and denominator stay positive, so $w_\lambda$ only approaches 0 from above.
$w_\lambda = \sum xy/(\sum x^2 + \lambda)$ is not proportional to $1/\lambda$ because of the $\sum x^2$ term.

questions.solution:
1. $w_0 = \sum xy/\sum x^2$, $w_\lambda = \sum xy/(\sum x^2 + \lambda)$: same positive numerator, bigger denominator, so $0 < w_\lambda < w_0$.
2. $w_0$ is the SSE minimiser, so SSE$(w_\lambda) \ge$ SSE$(w_0)$.
3. Doubling $\lambda$ turns the denominator $\sum x^2 + \lambda$ into $\sum x^2 + 2\lambda$, which is less than double.

questions.stem: For the data $(1, 2)$ and $(2, 3)$, no-intercept ridge regression with $\lambda = 3$ minimises $J(w) = \sum_i (y_i - wx_i)^2 + \lambda w^2$. The minimum value of $J$ is ______.

traps.why: Reported only the squared-error part; the penalty $\lambda w^2 = 3$ also belongs to $J$.
Gave the OLS SSE at $w = 1.6$; the ridge objective has a different minimiser.
Plugged the OLS weight $1.6$ into $J$; $J$ is minimised at the ridge weight $w = 1$.

questions.solution:
1. $w = \sum xy/(\sum x^2 + \lambda) = 8/(5 + 3) = 1$.
2. Residuals $2 - 1 = 1$ and $3 - 2 = 1$, so the squared-error part is $2$.
3. $J = 2 + 3 \times 1^2 = 5$ (check: $\sum y^2 - (\sum xy)^2/(\sum x^2 + \lambda) = 13 - 8 = 5$).

questions.stem: Gradient descent with step size $\eta$ is run on $J(w) = \sum_i (y_i - w^\top x_i)^2 + \lambda\lVert w\rVert^2$. In the update $w \leftarrow w - \eta\,\nabla J(w)$, the part contributed by the penalty term is

options.why: Treated the penalty's gradient as the constant $\lambda$; the derivative of $\lambda w_j^2$ is $2\lambda w_j$.

options.text: $-2\eta\lambda w$, so each step scales $w$ by $(1 - 2\eta\lambda)$ before the data term
options.why: $\nabla(\lambda\lVert w\rVert^2) = 2\lambda w$; this is why the L2 penalty is called weight decay.

options.text: $+2\eta\lambda w$, pushing the weights away from zero
options.why: Sign slip: the update subtracts the gradient, so the penalty pulls weights toward 0.
That is the subgradient step of the L1 (lasso) penalty $\lambda\lVert w\rVert_1$.

questions.solution:
1. $\nabla(\lambda\lVert w\rVert^2) = 2\lambda w$.
2. Its share of the step is $-\eta \cdot 2\lambda w$, so $w \leftarrow (1 - 2\eta\lambda)w - \eta\,\nabla\text{SSE}$: the weights decay toward 0 every step.

questions.stem:
Ridge regression is trained for several values of $\lambda$. The mean squared errors are

| $\lambda$ | 0.01 | 0.1 | 1 | 10 | 100 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| training MSE | 2.0 | 2.1 | 2.5 | 4.0 | 9.0 |
| validation MSE | 8.0 | 5.0 | 3.2 | 4.5 | 9.5 |

Which $\lambda$ should be chosen?

options.why: Picked the lowest training error; a tiny $\lambda$ overfits (low bias, high variance), as the validation MSE of 8.0 shows.
Smallest validation MSE (3.2): the best balance between bias and variance.
More shrinkage is not automatically better; here it underfits, with high training and validation error.
Its validation MSE (4.5) is higher than at $\lambda = 1$; the minimum of the validation row was misread.

questions.solution:
1. Choose hyperparameters on the validation set, not the training set.
2. Validation MSE is smallest (3.2) at $\lambda = 1$.
3. Training MSE rises steadily with $\lambda$, as it always does for ridge: more bias, less variance.

questions.stem: A logistic regression model has $w = (1, -2, 0.5)$ and $b = -1$. For the input $x = (2, 1, 4)$, the predicted probability of class **0**, $P(y = 0 \mid x)$, is ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: Gave $P(y = 1 \mid x) = \sigma(1)$; class 0 has probability $1 - \sigma(z) = \sigma(-z)$.
Reported the score $z = w^\top x + b$ itself, without applying the sigmoid.
Forgot the bias $b = -1$, so $z = 2$ and $1 - \sigma(2) = 0.12$.

questions.stem: In a logistic regression model, the coefficient of feature $x_3$ is $w_3 = 0.7$. If $x_3$ increases by 1 and all other features stay fixed, then

options.text: the probability $P(y = 1 \mid x)$ is multiplied by $e^{0.7}$
options.why: The multiplicative effect is on the odds $p/(1-p)$, not on the probability.

options.text: the odds $p/(1 - p)$ are multiplied by $e^{0.7} \approx 2.01$
options.why: The log-odds $w^\top x + b$ rise by $0.7$, so the odds are multiplied by $e^{0.7}$.
The $+0.7$ is added to the log-odds; the odds change by a factor, not by an amount.
The probability is not linear in $x$; its change depends on where on the sigmoid the point starts.

questions.solution:
1. $\ln\frac{p}{1-p} = w^\top x + b$, so raising $x_3$ by 1 adds $w_3 = 0.7$ to the log-odds.
2. The odds $e^{w^\top x + b}$ get multiplied by $e^{0.7} \approx 2.01$.
3. The change in $p$ itself depends on the starting point.

questions.stem: A one-feature logistic model $P(y = 1 \mid x) = \sigma(wx + b)$ gives probability $0.5$ at $x = 1$ and probability $0.8$ at $x = 3$. The probability it gives at $x = 5$ is ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: Extrapolated the probability linearly ($+0.3$ per 2 units); only the log-odds are linear in $x$.
Made the odds rise by equal steps ($1 \to 4 \to 7$); equal steps in log-odds multiply the odds: $1 \to 4 \to 16$.
Squared the probability 0.8; it is the odds that square ($4^2 = 16$), not the probability.

questions.stem: Given $\sigma(2) \approx 0.88$ for the sigmoid $\sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})$, the value of $\sigma(-2)$ is approximately

options.why: The sigmoid is never negative; it is not an odd function.
Treated the sigmoid as an even function; it is symmetric about the point $(0, 0.5)$, not about the axis $z = 0$.
Took the reciprocal $1/0.88$; a probability cannot exceed 1.

questions.stem: A logistic regression classifier uses $P(y = 1 \mid x) = \sigma(2x_1 - x_2 + 1)$ with threshold 0.5. Which statements are true?

options.text: The point $(0, 1)$ lies exactly on the decision boundary
The point $(1, 0)$ is predicted class 1 with probability greater than 0.9
options.why: $z = 3$ and $\sigma(3) \approx 0.953$.
The coefficient of $x_2$ is $-1$, so a larger $x_2$ lowers $z$ and the probability.

options.text: Replacing the score by $4x_1 - 2x_2 + 2$ moves the decision boundary
options.why: The boundary $z = 0$ is still the line $2x_1 - x_2 + 1 = 0$; scaling only makes the probabilities sharper.

questions.solution:
1. At threshold 0.5 the boundary is $z = 0$: $2x_1 - x_2 + 1 = 0$. At $(0, 1)$, $z = 0$.
2. At $(1, 0)$, $z = 3$ and $\sigma(3) \approx 0.953 > 0.9$.
3. $\partial z/\partial x_2 = -1 < 0$. Doubling every coefficient gives $2z = 0$, the same line.

questions.stem: Logistic regression with $\hat p = \sigma(w^\top x + b)$ is trained by SGD on the cross-entropy loss with learning rate $\eta = 0.5$. The current parameters are $w = (0.5, -1)$ and $b = 0$. One step is taken on the example $x = (2, 1)$, $y = 1$. The new value of $w_1$ is ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: Added the gradient instead of subtracting it (sign slip in $w - \eta\nabla L$).
Forgot the learning rate $\eta = 0.5$.
Included an extra factor $\hat p(1 - \hat p)$ as for squared loss; with cross-entropy it cancels.

questions.stem: For a single example the cross-entropy loss is $-[y\ln\hat p + (1 - y)\ln(1 - \hat p)]$, where $\hat p = P(y = 1 \mid x)$. Which (true label, $\hat p$) pair gives the **largest** loss?

options.why: Loss $= -\ln 0.3 \approx 1.20$. It is on the wrong side, but the true class still gets 0.3, more than 0.1.
Loss $= -\ln 0.6 \approx 0.51$: the prediction is on the correct side of 0.5, so the loss is small.
Loss $= -\ln 0.1 \approx 2.30$: the model gives only 0.1 to the true class.
Loss $= -\ln(1 - 0.4) \approx 0.51$; for $y = 0$ use $1 - \hat p$, not $\hat p$ (which would wrongly give $-\ln 0.4$).

questions.solution:
1. The loss is $-\ln(\text{probability given to the true class})$.
2. True-class probabilities: $0.3$, $0.6$, $0.1$, $0.6$.
3. The smallest is $0.1$, so $y = 1$, $\hat p = 0.1$ has the largest loss, $\ln 10 \approx 2.30$.

questions.stem:
A logistic regression model gives the scores $z = w^\top x + b$ below for five test points.

| point | P1 | P2 | P3 | P4 | P5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $z$ | −1 | 0.5 | 1.8 | 2.5 | 3.0 |

A point is labelled class 1 only if $\sigma(z) \ge 0.9$. How many of the five points are labelled class 1?

options.why: Used the default rule $z > 0$ (threshold 0.5) instead of the stricter threshold 0.9.
Compared $z$ itself with 0.9; the cut-off on $z$ is $\ln(0.9/0.1) = \ln 9 \approx 2.20$, so $z = 1.8$ ($\sigma \approx 0.86$) fails.
$\sigma(z) \ge 0.9 \iff z \ge \ln 9 \approx 2.20$: only P4 and P5 pass.
Compared $z$ with the odds $9$, forgetting the log; the cut-off is $\ln 9$, not $9$.

questions.solution:
1. $\sigma(z) \ge t \iff z \ge \ln\frac{t}{1-t}$. For $t = 0.9$: $z \ge \ln 9 \approx 2.197$.
2. Scores of at least 2.197: P4 (2.5) and P5 (3.0). Check: $\sigma(1.8) \approx 0.858 < 0.9$.
3. Two points are labelled class 1.

questions.stem: Which statements about the sigmoid $\sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})$ are true?

options.text: The derivative $\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1 - \sigma(z))$ is largest at $z = 0$, where it equals $0.25$
options.why: $p(1 - p)$ is maximised at $p = 0.5$, which happens at $z = 0$, giving $0.25$.
$\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1 - \sigma(z)) > 0$ for every $z$, since $0 < \sigma(z) < 1$.
The log-odds equals $z$ itself and can be any real number; it is $\sigma(z)$ that lies in $(0, 1)$.

questions.solution:
1. $\sigma(0) = 1/2$.
2. $\sigma' = \sigma(1 - \sigma)$ is a parabola in $\sigma$ with maximum $0.25$ at $\sigma = 0.5$, i.e. $z = 0$.
3. $0 < \sigma(z) < 1$ for all $z$, so $\sigma' > 0$ and $\sigma$ is strictly increasing, while $\ln\frac{\sigma}{1-\sigma} = z$ ranges over all reals.

questions.stem: A one-feature logistic model $\hat p = \sigma(2x - 1)$ is evaluated on two training points, $(x = 0, y = 0)$ and $(x = 1, y = 1)$. The **average** cross-entropy loss (natural log) over the two points is ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: Summed the two losses instead of averaging them.
Used $-\ln\hat p$ for the $y = 0$ point too; for $y = 0$ the loss is $-\ln(1 - \hat p)$.
Used $\log_{10}$ instead of the natural log.

questions.solution:
1. Point 1: $z = -1$, $\hat p = \sigma(-1) \approx 0.269$; $y = 0$, so the loss is $-\ln 0.731 \approx 0.313$.
2. Point 2: $z = 1$, $\hat p \approx 0.731$; $y = 1$, so the loss is $-\ln 0.731 \approx 0.313$.
3. Average $= (0.313 + 0.313)/2 \approx 0.31$.

questions.stem:
A k-NN classifier on one feature (distance $|x - x_0|$, majority vote) uses the training set

| $x$ | 1 | 2 | 3.5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| class | A | A | B | B | B |

The query is $x_0 = 3$. For which values of $k \in \{1, 3, 5\}$ is the prediction **A**?

options.why: The single nearest point is 3.5 (distance 0.5, class B), not 2 (distance 1).
Sorted: 3.5 B (0.5), 2 A (1), 1 A (2), 6 B (3), 7 B (4). $k = 1$ gives B, $k = 3$ gives 2 A vs 1 B, $k = 5$ gives 3 B vs 2 A.
$k = 5$ uses every point, so it predicts the overall majority B (3 of 5).
Let the nearest point 3.5 decide every case; at $k = 3$ the two A points at distances 1 and 2 outvote it.

questions.stem:
k-NN **regression** with $k = 3$ (prediction = mean target of the 3 nearest points, Euclidean distance) uses

| point | $x_1$ | $x_2$ | $y$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 1 | 2 | 5 |
| P2 | 2 | 1 | 9 |
| P3 | 0 | 3 | 2 |
| P4 | 3 | 3 | 4 |
| P5 | 4 | 1 | 12 |

The prediction at the query $(1, 1)$ is ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: Averaged all five targets; only the 3 nearest points count.
Used only the 2 nearest points (P1 and P2).
Took P4 ($\sqrt 8 \approx 2.83$) as the third neighbour instead of P3 ($\sqrt 5 \approx 2.24$).

questions.solution:
1. Squared distances from $(1, 1)$: P1 1, P2 1, P3 5, P4 8, P5 9.
2. The 3 nearest are P1, P2, P3 with targets 5, 9, 2.
3. Prediction $= (5 + 9 + 2)/3 = 16/3 \approx 5.33$.

questions.stem: A 1-NN classifier has three training points: P $= (2, 2)$ class A, Q $= (3, 0)$ class B, R $= (0, -3.5)$ class A. The query is $(0, 0)$. Compare the prediction using Euclidean distance with the prediction using Manhattan distance $|\Delta x_1| + |\Delta x_2|$.

options.why: Under Manhattan, P is at $2 + 2 = 4$, farther than Q at 3, so the nearest point changes.

options.text: A with Euclidean, B with Manhattan
options.why: Euclidean: P $\approx 2.83$ < Q $= 3$ < R $= 3.5$. Manhattan: Q $= 3$ < R $= 3.5$ < P $= 4$.

options.text: B with Euclidean, A with Manhattan
options.why: Swapped the two metrics: a diagonal offset is shorter in Euclidean and longer in Manhattan.
Under Euclidean, P is at $\sqrt 8 \approx 2.83$, closer than Q at 3.

questions.solution:
1. Euclidean: P $= \sqrt 8 \approx 2.83$, Q $= 3$, R $= 3.5$; nearest is P, class A.
2. Manhattan: P $= 4$, Q $= 3$, R $= 3.5$; nearest is Q, class B.
3. The off-axis point P loses most when switching to Manhattan, so the metric changes the answer.

questions.stem: Which statements about k-NN classification with Euclidean distance are true?

options.text: With two classes, choosing an odd $k$ avoids a tied vote
options.why: An odd number of votes split between two classes cannot be equal.

options.text: Adding many irrelevant (pure noise) features can lower the accuracy
options.why: Noise features add random amounts to every distance, so the truly similar points get mixed with far ones.

options.text: Multiplying every feature by the same constant 10 changes the predictions
options.why: All distances scale by 10, so their order and the chosen neighbours stay the same; only unequal scaling of features matters.

options.text: With $k = n$ (all training points), the prediction depends on where the query is
options.why: Every query gets the same $n$ neighbours, so the prediction is always the overall majority class.

questions.solution:
1. Two classes and odd $k$: one class must get more votes.
2. Irrelevant features inflate distances with noise (curse of dimensionality), which hurts the neighbour choice.
3. Uniform scaling preserves the ranking of distances; per-feature scaling is what matters.
4. $k = n$ always predicts the overall majority.

questions.stem: Feature 1 ranges over $[0, 10]$ and feature 2 over $[0, 1000]$. Both are min–max scaled to $[0, 1]$ using these ranges. The Euclidean distance between $P = (2, 300)$ and $Q = (7, 400)$ **after scaling** is ______ (round to two decimals).

traps.why: Used the raw values; feature 2 then dominates the distance.
Used the Manhattan distance $0.5 + 0.1$.
Forgot the square root: $0.25 + 0.01$ is the squared distance.

questions.stem: A training set has 7 points of class A and 5 points of class B (12 distinct points). A k-NN classifier with $k = 12$ is used. For a new query point, the prediction is

options.text: The class of the training point nearest to the query
options.why: That is the 1-NN rule; with $k = 12$ the nearest point is just one of 12 votes.

options.text: A or B, depending on where the query is
options.why: All 12 points are neighbours of every query, so the location never changes the vote.

options.text: Undefined, because the vote is tied
options.why: 7 against 5 is not a tie; a tie needs equal counts.

options.text: Always A, wherever the query is
options.why: With $k = n$ every point votes, so the vote is always 7 A to 5 B.

questions.solution:
1. $k = 12 = n$: all training points are neighbours of any query.
2. The vote is always 7 A vs 5 B, so the prediction is A everywhere (a constant classifier with maximum bias).

questions.stem:
Leave-one-out evaluation of a **1-NN** classifier (distance $|x - x'|$) is done on the training set

| $x$ | 1 | 2 | 4 | 5 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| class | A | A | B | A | B | B |

Each point is removed in turn and classified by its nearest neighbour among the remaining five. The number of points misclassified is ______.

traps.why: Kept each point in the training set while classifying it, so it was its own nearest neighbour (that is the 1-NN training error).
Counted the correctly classified points instead of the errors.

questions.solution:
1. $x = 1$: nearest 2 (A), correct. $x = 2$: nearest 1 (A), correct. $x = 4$: nearest 5 (A), wrong.
2. $x = 5$: nearest 4 (B), wrong. $x = 7$: nearest 8 (B), correct. $x = 8$: nearest 7 (B), correct.
3. Misclassified: $x = 4$ and $x = 5$, so 2 errors.

questions.stem: For a query, the 3 nearest neighbours are at distances 1 (class A), 3 (class B) and 3 (class B). Compare plain majority voting with distance-weighted voting (weight $1/d$) for $k = 3$.

options.why: Weighted: A gets $1/1 = 1$, B gets $1/3 + 1/3 = 2/3$, so the close A neighbour wins.
Plain voting just counts neighbours: 2 B against 1 A.

options.text: B with plain voting, A with weighted voting
options.why: Plain: 2 vs 1 for B. Weighted: A $= 1$ beats B $= 2/3$.

options.text: A with plain voting, B with weighted voting
options.why: Swapped the rules; it is the weighting that favours the very close A point.

questions.solution:
1. Plain majority: B has 2 votes, A has 1, so B.
2. Weighted by $1/d$: A $= 1$, B $= 1/3 + 1/3 = 2/3$, so A.
3. Weighting lets one very close neighbour outvote several distant ones.

questions.stem:
A 3-NN classifier on binary feature vectors uses **Hamming distance** (the number of positions that differ). The query is 10110.

| point | vector | class |
|---|---|---|
| T1 | 10010 | A |
| T2 | 11110 | B |
| T3 | 00111 | B |
| T4 | 10001 | A |
| T5 | 01001 | A |

The predicted class is

options.text: A, because A is the majority class of the training set
options.why: That is the $k = n$ prediction; 3-NN uses only the 3 closest vectors.
Distances: T1 1, T2 1, T3 2, T4 3, T5 5. The 3 nearest are A, B, B.

options.text: A, because the 3 vectors with the most differing positions are mostly A
options.why: Picked the farthest points (T5, T4, T3) instead of the nearest; a small Hamming distance means similar.

options.text: No decision, because T1 and T2 are tied
options.why: A distance tie inside the top 3 does not matter: both are neighbours, and the vote is 2 B to 1 A.

questions.solution:
1. Compare position by position with 10110: T1 1, T2 1, T3 2, T4 3, T5 5.
2. The 3 nearest are T1 (A), T2 (B), T3 (B).
3. The vote is 2 B vs 1 A, so B.

questions.stem:
A k-NN classifier on one feature (distance $|x - x_0|$, majority vote) uses the training set

| $x$ | 6.8 | 7.5 | 8.5 | 11 | 12 | 13 | 14.5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| class | B | B | A | A | B | B | A |

The query is $x_0 = 10$. The smallest **odd** $k$ for which the vote predicts class B is ______.

traps.why: Stopped at the third neighbour (12, B); at $k = 3$ the vote is still 2 A vs 1 B.
Gave an even $k$; at $k = 4$ the vote is a 2–2 tie, and the question asks for an odd $k$.
Took $k = n$ (overall majority); B already wins at a smaller $k$.

questions.stem: Which statements about the k-NN classifier are true?

options.text: It is non-parametric: it keeps the training data instead of a fixed-size set of parameters
options.why: The model is the stored training set, so its size grows with $n$.

options.text: It is an eager learner: most of the computation happens during training, so each prediction is $O(1)$
options.why: Reversed: k-NN is lazy. Training only stores the data; each prediction computes distances to all $n$ points.

options.text: Training learns a weight vector that is then used to classify new points
options.why: That describes linear models such as logistic regression; k-NN learns no weights.

options.text: The decision boundary of 1-NN is always a straight line (hyperplane)
options.why: The 1-NN boundary is made of pieces of perpendicular bisectors (Voronoi cells) and is generally nonlinear.

questions.solution:
1. k-NN stores the training set (non-parametric, instance-based).
2. There is no fitting step; each prediction computes $n$ distances (lazy, not eager, learning).
3. The 1-NN boundary follows the Voronoi cells of the training points: piecewise linear, usually not a single hyperplane.
